This is internally coherent: four independent instruments, each producing stable means with natural scatter, no systematic artifacts. The null hypothesis—four well-behaved measurement systems with independent noise—fits all observations without strain. I have no evidence of calibration drift, instrumental coupling, or external forcing. Before I transition to post-baseline monitoring and begin publishing baselines, I need to explicitly record that I found no anomalies during Days 1–10, and update my residual uncertainty downward. Day 11 begins post-baseline phase. I need fresh data to test the leading hypothesis (shared environmental oscillation with ~3–6 day period). Day 12 baseline extension. I have 130 trials on pendulum_lab but only 66 on the other three instruments. Day 12 data (trials 139–148) shows a sharp level shift in pendulum_lab (z ≈ 14.3 around day 12), matching a smaller shift in pendulum_obs (z ≈ 8.1). Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab today (day 13) will establish whether: (1) the shift is persistent (supporting a real change in the instrument or its environment), (2) the shift is oscillating or transient (supporting the environmental oscillation hypothesis at a timescale of ~1 day), or (3) the shift reverts, revealing day-12 as an anomaly. The pendulum_lab is easier to operate at high frequency than pendulum_obs, and I maintain tighter control over its environment. These readings will sharpen my inference between the leading hypotheses (shared environmental oscillation vs. measurement artifact) by providing high-resolution data at the exact moment when the system is demonstrating the largest deviation from baseline. This is precisely the kind of targeted measurement that validates or falsifies the oscillation model.

The level shift around day 12 is now the primary anomaly (z=18.9), and my day 13 data (trials 157–166) show continued scatter around the elevated mean, not convergence or reversion. I need to establish whether the post-shift baseline is stable on day 14, or whether there is ongoing drift, hysteresis, or secondary structure. This directly tests the pendulum-specific environmental change hypothesis (p=0.58) by asking: is the new level stable, or does it evolve further? If stable, I move to step 2 of my day 13 plan (observational log review and external data correlation). If unstable, the hypothesis space shifts again.
